Bandwidth's accepted definition is the weighted standard deviation of frequency bins around the centroid, computed over the per-bin energy values. The note's removal argument ('normalization of power values fails') names the wrong object: the normalization denominator is the sum of the same per-bin vector — a one-line reduction of the distribution, not the scalar construct. Remove the scalar total and bandwidth still operates: recompute the sum from the vector in one step. The real anchor is already accepted — bandwidth DEPENDS_ON spectral-band-distribution — which carries exactly this claim. A denominator computed from the same vector is not a separate operational dependency; this is the same denominator pattern the court struck on the standardized-moment edges (band-skew/band-kurt -> band-variance, Oct 12).

The band variant's own accepted definition defeats the removal test: spectral-band-flux is 'the absolute difference of spectral-band-energy between consecutive frames' — it operates on the scalar band-energy values at two frame times, not on the per-bin vector. Remove the per-bin distribution and the band-flux computation still runs: the pipeline stores the band-energy scalar per frame, and the subtraction of two stored scalars needs no bins. The note's 'no signal to iterate' misstates the definition — there is no iteration over bins in the band variant. Its accepted anchor DEPENDS_ON spectral-band-energy already carries the true substrate claim, and that edge stands. The distribution dependency is inherited, not direct: the scalar is the operative input to this statistic as defined.
